# Regularization and Geometry Constraints

Also called: Regularization and Artifact Reduction, Geometric Priors in 3DGS

## Overview
Regularization and Geometry Constraints address the inherent ambiguity of single-view or sparse-view reconstruction in [3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)](#1174-3d-gaussian-splatting-3dgs.md), where color-only supervision often leads to incorrect Gaussian positioning, floating artifacts, or collapsed geometry [S1, S3]. This family of methods introduces auxiliary loss terms or structural constraints to enforce geometric plausibility, spectral consistency, or physical priors, distinguishing itself from sibling methods like [Base 3DGS Optimization](7549-base-3dgs-optimization.md) which relies solely on photometric reconstruction loss. Unlike [Physical Parameter Optimization](4111-physical-parameter-optimization.md) which optimizes physical properties, these constraints directly guide the optimization trajectory of centers, opacities, and shapes to prevent overfitting and improve structural fidelity [S1, S3].

## Shared principles
All methods in this family compute a differentiable auxiliary loss term $\mathcal{L}_{reg}$ that is added to the total training loss:
$$ \mathcal{L}_{total} = \mathcal{L}_{rgb} + \lambda_{reg} \mathcal{L}_{reg} $$
where $\lambda_{reg}$ is a scalar weight. The core mechanism involves extracting a geometric or spectral property from the rendered output (or the input data) and comparing it against a target or constraint. The gradients of $\mathcal{L}_{reg}$ flow back through the differentiable rasterizer to update the Gaussian parameters $\theta$ (centers $\mu$, scales $s$, rotations $q$, opacities $\alpha$, and colors $c$) [Parent].

## Subtopics

### [Frequency Regularization](6130-frequency-regularization.md)
[Frequency regularization](#6130-frequency-regularization.md) is a training-time technique that constrains the spectral content of the rendered output to guide [Gaussian densification](#4314-gaussian-densification.md) toward high-frequency regions. It solves the problem where standard 3DGS initialization and densification may fail to capture fine geometric details or high-frequency textures, leading to blurry reconstructions. Unlike [Smoothed 2D Supervision](7213-smoothed-2d-supervision.md) which operates in the spatial domain via kernel smoothing, or [Depth Regularization](7616-depth-regularization.md) which enforces geometric consistency, frequency regularization operates in the spectral domain to explicitly encourage the representation of high-frequency signal components. See [Frequency Regularization](6130-frequency-regularization.md).

### [Smoothed 2D Supervision](7213-smoothed-2d-supervision.md)
[Smoothed 2D Supervision](#7213-smoothed-2d-supervision.md) stabilizes the joint optimization of camera poses and 3D radiance fields by blurring 2D training images with scheduled 2D Gaussian kernels. It produces smoothed image gradients to prevent noisy gradient updates and restricts the high-frequency spectrum of the learned scene. Unlike [Frequency Regularization](6130-frequency-regularization.md) which operates in the frequency domain, this method applies spatial-domain smoothing directly to the target images before loss computation. See [Smoothed 2D Supervision](7213-smoothed-2d-supervision.md).

### [Depth Regularization](7616-depth-regularization.md)
[Depth regularization](#7616-depth-regularization.md) methods enforce geometric plausibility in [differentiable volume rendering](#43-differentiable-volume-rendering.md) by minimizing the discrepancy between rendered depth maps and external depth targets (monocular estimates, stereo matches, or LiDAR). This family addresses the inherent ambiguity of single-view or sparse-view reconstruction, where color-only supervision often leads to incorrect Gaussian positioning, floating artifacts, or collapsed geometry. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like [Frequency Regularization](6130-frequency-regularization.md) or [Smoothed 2D Supervision](7213-smoothed-2d-supervision.md) by operating directly on the geometric depth channel rather than color space or frequency domains, providing explicit metric or relative depth constraints. See [Depth Regularization](7616-depth-regularization.md).

### [3D Half-Gaussian Splatting Covariance Transformation and Regularization](9150-3d-half-gaussian-splatting-covariance-transformation-and-reg.md)
[3D Half-Gaussian Splatting](#9011-3d-half-gaussian-splatting.md) (3D-HGS) modifies the standard 3D Gaussian kernel into a half-ellipsoid to better model sharp surface boundaries and occlusions, addressing the "blooming" artifacts common in full Gaussians near object edges. It achieves this by transforming the covariance matrix into a local basis aligned with a splitting plane normal, projecting the covariance to enforce zero variance along the normal direction, and then transforming it back to [world space](#2511-voxel-coordinate-systems-and-conversion.md). This method builds on [Regularization and Geometry Constraints](6269-regularization-and-geometry-constraints.md) by applying a structural constraint to the Gaussian parameters themselves rather than an auxiliary loss term. See [3D Half-Gaussian Splatting Covariance Transformation and Regularization](9150-3d-half-gaussian-splatting-covariance-transformation-and-reg.md).

### [Hard and Soft Depth Regularization](9178-hard-and-soft-depth-regularization.md)
[Hard and Soft Depth Regularization](#9178-hard-and-soft-depth-regularization.md) is a technique for constraining the geometry of 3D [Gaussian Splatting](#946-gaussian-splatting.md) by encouraging spatial reshaping (movement of centers) rather than deforming Gaussian shapes, thereby preventing detail loss and blurred appearance caused by forcing anisotropic Gaussians to fit smooth monocular depth. It sets itself apart from standard depth regularization methods by decoupling the optimization of center positions and opacities through two distinct rendered depth maps, while freezing shape parameters (scale and rotation) during the process. This approach addresses the conflict where NeRF-style depth regularization forces [primitive geometry](#6264-primitive-geometry.md) to conform to smooth estimates, which conflicts with complex color appearance. See [Hard and Soft Depth Regularization](9178-hard-and-soft-depth-regularization.md).

#### Wild-GS
Wild-GS aligns pixel appearance features from image triplanes directly to 3D Gaussians and uses depth regularization and visibility maps to mitigate transient effects and constrain geometry [S1].

#### Source Feature Extrapolation
Source Feature Extrapolation improves extrapolation capabilities beyond source view frustums by padding source images and adding [positional encoding](#876-positional-encoding.md) channels for padded regions, preventing smearing artifacts in regions not visible by source images [S2]. It applies border padding to source images $I^{(i)}$ and creates a channel $\Gamma$ containing pixel-wise positional encodings for padded regions: $\Gamma[u,v] = \gamma(u,v)$ if $(u,v)$ is not in $I^{(i)}$, else $0$. The modified input is $I'(i) = \text{concatenate}(I_{pad}, \Gamma)$, where $\gamma(\cdot)$ denotes positional encoding with exponential frequencies [S2].

#### SDF-Regularized 3DGS
SDF-Regularized 3DGS improves geometric fidelity by imposing physical constraints, such as [Signed Distance Fields](#1466-signed-distance-fields-sdf.md) (SDFs), monocular depth priors, or multi-view geometric constraints, during optimization [S3]. It introduces a regularization term to minimize the difference between an ideal SDF and the SDF calculated from Gaussians, often using a dual-branch framework with GS- and SDF-branches jointly optimized to provide mutual guidance [S3]. It may also incorporate geometric regularization such as monocular depth priors or multi-plane Gaussian optimization [S3].

#### FreGS
FreGS applies progressive frequency regularization to primitives to prevent overfitting and high-frequency artifacts during training [S4, unofficial].

## Background
The original [3D Gaussian Splatting method](#4010-gaussian-kernel-volumetric-primitive.md) optimizes for photometric loss, often resulting in unstructured density clouds that do not represent a valid surface [S3]. To recover high-quality geometry, recent methods impose physical constraints during optimization [S3]. This includes integrating Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) [YLX*24, GL24], using monocular depth priors [LZB*24, COL24], or applying frequency regularization to ensure consistent appearance across resolutions [S4, unofficial]. Popping artifacts arising from depth-sorting steps have also been addressed by [hybrid transparency blending](#3294-hybrid-transparency.md) or [ray-tracing kernels](#5968-ray-tracing-kernel.md) [S4, unofficial]. The survey [S4, unofficial] notes that methods like FreGS [78] apply progressive frequency regularization, while others like Faster-GS [79] stabilize convergence by rescaling scaling gradients. [ABSGS](#6127-absgs.md) [80] sharpens edges by back-propagating only high-frequency residuals.
